text: I'm a mother on a very tight budget: about four hundred dollars a month, for everything. I built MamaPal because I needed it.
Pal cares: it knows your baby's month. Pal cuts: it keeps what the baby really needs. Pal claims: it finds the money you're owed. All of it runs on PayPal and Claude.
Every morning Pal says the whole month in five lines: what's left, what BIT needs, how the pantry looks, what help I can claim, and what it saved me last time.

I type what the feed told me to buy. Pal reads the rash, keeps a two-dollar pharmacy cream and a ten-dollar cotton sleep sack, and tells me why in one line each. A hundred and five dollars becomes twelve.
Pal is nobody's shop. It checks the whole web and shows real listings with links. If it finds cheaper, the cart goes down.
One PayPal button, for exactly that. Sandbox, but real: every payment leaves a capture ID in the ledger, and the pantry updates.
Plan is Pal cares. Five hundred items from pregnancy to school, by stage. Each one opens: what it is, which size, how much, the traps, and today's prices from real stores.
Pal claims. From my ZIP and income it found about fifteen hundred dollars a month I can apply for, with the one rule that decides each program and the steps to do it.
And a twenty-second brand survey pays three dollars straight into my PayPal.
Me is BIT's story and my records: where he is, what we spent, month by month. Count every dollar. Live every day.
MamaPal. Pal cares, Pal cuts, Pal claims. For every mother's hardest month.
